Roth, Daguang Xu, David Bericat, Ralf Floca, S. Kevin Zhou, Haris Shuaib, Keyvan Farahani, Klaus H. Maier-Hein, Stephen Aylward, Prerna Dogra, Sebastien Ourselin, Andrew Feng

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Introduces MONAI, an open-source, community-supported PyTorch-based framework for deep learning in healthcare, providing domain-optimized tools for medical imaging, including network architectures, transforms, loss functions, and workflows.
contribution_summary.novelty: The novelty lies in the comprehensive, standardized, and modular framework that unifies fragmented healthcare AI development, with a focus on medical imaging and reproducibility.
strengths: Open-source and freely available (Apache-2.0 license).
Provides a wide range of domain-specific transforms, networks, and loss functions.
Designed to be PyTorch-native, ensuring ease of use and integration.
Strong community support and consortium-led development.
Includes utilities for reproducibility, determinism, and interpretability.
weaknesses: Not a specific organ segmentation study; lacks experimental validation on CT organ segmentation.
No quantitative results or comparisons with state-of-the-art segmentation methods.
No discussion of clinical applicability or performance on real-world datasets.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: The framework itself is highly applicable for developing clinical segmentation models, but the paper does not demonstrate direct clinical applicability or validation.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Training set sizes: 50 for CT (not >50), 60 for MRI, 1800 for endoscopy, 1000 for microscopy. The CT dataset is exactly 50, which is not >50, but other datasets have larger sizes, so partial.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: All datasets are clearly described: Abdomen CT from FLARE Challenge, Abdomen MRI from AMOS Challenge, Endoscopy from EndoVis Challenge, Microscopy from Cell Segmentation Challenge. Sources and origins are specified.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Train/test splits are clearly described for all datasets, but validation split is not explicitly mentioned; they likely use training data for validation or rely on nnU-Net's self-configuring, but not specified.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Annotation processes are described: CT annotations from AbdomenCT-1K and challenge organizers; MRI annotations generated by radiologists with MedSAM and ITK-SNAP; endoscopy and microscopy from official challenges.

Q5_external_validation.justification: All tasks use independent test sets: CT test from different centers, MRI test newly annotated, endoscopy test from unseen videos, microscopy test from challenge. External validation is performed.

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The U-Mamba block, encoder-decoder structure, Mamba block details, residual blocks, and overall network are fully described with a figure.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: They specify optimizer (SGD), loss function, epochs, patch size, batch size, but do not provide learning rate, momentum, weight decay, etc. They rely on nnU-Net's default hyperparameters, which are not fully detailed.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function is unweighted sum of Dice and cross-entropy, justified by robustness across tasks (reference provided).

Q9_preprocessing.justification: They mention using default nnU-Net preprocessing and post-processing for instance segmentation (converting to semantic and then labeling), but do not describe the preprocessing steps in detail.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Code, models, and data are publicly available at https://wanglab.ai/u-mamba.html.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Uses DSC and NSD for semantic tasks, and F1 for instance segmentation, thus multiple metrics.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: They report mean ± standard deviation, but no confidence intervals or p-values.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compares with nnU-Net, SegResNet, UNETR, and SwinUNETR, which are state-of-the-art methods.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-organ results are provided in Appendix Tables 5, 6, and 7 for CT and MRI.

Q15_limitations.justification: They discuss limitations such as training from scratch for Transformers, potential for ensemble, and future work, but do not explicitly analyze failure cases.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Low - Patient selection is defined by public challenge datasets with clear inclusion criteria.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Consistent evaluation protocols, same preprocessing, and metrics across all methods; training from scratch is acknowledged.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (DSC, NSD, F1) and per-organ results are reported.

detailed_extraction.title: U-Mamba: Enhancing Long-range Dependency for Biomedical Image Segmentation
detailed_extraction.authors: Jun Ma, Feifei Li, Bo Wang

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Proposes U-Mamba, a hybrid CNN-SSM architecture that combines local feature extraction of CNNs with long-range dependency modeling of Mamba (SSM) for biomedical image segmentation, achieving superior performance over CNN and Transformer baselines on multiple tasks.
contribution_summary.novelty: Integrates Mamba blocks into a U-Net-like encoder-decoder, leveraging the linear scaling of SSMs to capture long-range dependencies efficiently. Inherits nnU-Net's self-configuring mechanism for automatic adaptation to different datasets.
strengths: Outperforms state-of-the-art CNN and Transformer methods on 3D CT/MRI organ segmentation, 2D instrument segmentation, and cell segmentation.
Publicly available code, models, and data.
Extensive evaluation across diverse modalities and tasks with per-organ results.
Efficient linear complexity compared to quadratic self-attention in Transformers.
weaknesses: Training from scratch may disadvantage Transformer baselines; no pre-training used.
No statistical significance testing (only standard deviations).
Relies on nnU-Net defaults for many hyperparameters, limiting reproducibility details.
Limited discussion of failure cases and edge scenarios.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: U-Mamba can be used for accurate organ segmentation in CT and MRI, instrument segmentation in endoscopy, and cell segmentation in microscopy, potentially improving clinical workflows by providing robust and efficient segmentation with fewer outliers.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: The paper curates a dataset of 11,454 CT scans, which is far above the 50-subject threshold.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Sources are clearly described, including in-house and public datasets (e.g., TCIA, MSD, TotalSegmentator, etc.) with a detailed table in the supplementary.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: Each data source is randomly split into 64% training, 16% validation, and 20% test sets, which is explicit.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: The paper describes the use of manual labels, pseudo-labels from TotalSegmentator, and supervoxels from SAM, but does not detail the manual annotation process (e.g., who annotated, inter-observer variability).

Q5_external_validation.justification: External validation is performed on multiple independent datasets for zero-shot (murine, C4KC-KITS, Adrenocortical Carcinoma, Hepatocellular Carcinoma) and finetuning (WORD).

Q6_architecture_description.justification: The architecture is fully described: SegResNet backbone, two branches (automatic and interactive), point head with cross-attention, class embeddings, and merging algorithm.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Training details are partially given (patch size, GPU count, total GPU hours), but key hyperparameters like learning rate, optimizer, and loss function specifics are not provided.

Q8_loss_function.justification: The loss function is not specified or justified; only 'LossFunction' is mentioned in the algorithms.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre/post-processing steps are partially described: sliding window inference, patch-based training, resampling for speed, and a merging algorithm for interactive refinement, but full preprocessing (e.g., intensity normalization) is not detailed.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Code and weights are publicly available at https://github.com/Project-MONAI/VISTA.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Only Dice score is used as the segmentation metric; no other metrics (e.g., IoU, surface distance) are reported.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: No confidence intervals, p-values, or statistical significance tests are reported.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Comparisons are made with state-of-the-art methods including Auto3DSeg, nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, MedSAM, SegVol, and SAM2.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-class results are provided in the supplementary material, although the main table shows per-dataset averages.

Q15_limitations.justification: Limitations are discussed in the conclusion (e.g., need for more classes, modalities, clinical validation), but specific failure cases of VISTA3D are not explicitly analyzed.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection is not explicitly defined; the study uses a mix of public and in-house datasets with varying protocols, but inclusion/exclusion criteria are not detailed.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Outcomes are assessed consistently using the same Dice metric and test splits across all datasets.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - All relevant outcomes (automatic, interactive, zero-shot, finetuning) are reported, with per-class details in supplementary.

detailed_extraction.title: VISTA3D: A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
detailed_extraction.authors: Yufan He, Pengfei Guo, Yucheng Tang, Andriy Myronenko, Vishwesh Nath, Ziyue Xu, Dong Yang, Can Zhao, Benjamin Simon, Mason Belue, Stephanie Harmon, Baris Turkbey, Daguang Xu, Wenqi Li

contribution_summary.main_contribution: VISTA3D is a unified 3D segmentation foundation model that supports automatic segmentation of 127 classes, interactive segmentation with point clicks, zero-shot segmentation of novel classes, and few-shot finetuning. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on both automatic and interactive tasks across 14 datasets.
contribution_summary.novelty: The paper introduces a novel 3D supervoxel method to distill knowledge from 2D SAM for 3D zero-shot performance, a four-stage training recipe, and a unified architecture that combines automatic and interactive branches with a merging algorithm for efficient human correction.
strengths: Large-scale dataset curation (11,454 CT scans) with diverse labels.
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets and baselines.
Publicly available code and weights.
Strong performance in automatic, interactive, zero-shot, and few-shot settings.
Practical human-in-the-loop workflow design.
weaknesses: Only Dice score is used for evaluation; no other metrics or statistical analysis.
Loss function and key hyperparameters are not specified, limiting reproducibility.
Preprocessing details are incomplete.
Failure cases are not explicitly analyzed.
Manual annotation process is not described in detail.
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: VISTA3D can significantly reduce human effort in clinical workflows by providing accurate automatic segmentation for common organs, allowing interactive correction, and enabling zero-shot segmentation of novel structures. It is particularly useful for large cohort analysis and surgical planning, though further clinical validation is needed.

Q1_dataset_size.justification: Trained on 120+ datasets with 64,518 volumes, far exceeding the 50-subject threshold.

Q2_dataset_source.justification: Datasets are publicly available and clearly referenced (CT, MRI, PET, microscopy, etc.) with specific citations.

Q3_train_test_split.justification: 5% of images held out for internal validation; external test sets (RadioActive benchmark and OOD datasets) are clearly defined.

Q4_ground_truth.justification: Ground truth comes from existing public datasets; annotation process not described in detail, but pseudo-labels via SAM/SAM2 are explained.

Q5_external_validation.justification: Evaluated on held-out RadioActive benchmark and multiple out-of-distribution datasets (microCT, knee MRI, insect anatomy, PET).

Q6_architecture_description.justification: Architecture based on nnU-Net with ResEnc-L backbone and early prompting strategy; sufficiently described.

Q7_reproducibility.justification: Training details (optimizer, learning rate, epochs) not provided; only interaction simulation and general training pipeline are described.

Q8_loss_function.justification: Loss function is not specified or justified in the paper.

Q9_preprocessing.justification: Pre-processing (normalization) not detailed; post-processing (AutoZoom, sliding window refinement) is described.

Q10_code_availability.justification: Code and models are publicly available via Napari plugin, MITK integration, and Python backend.

Q11_multiple_metrics.justification: Uses Dice and AUC (for interactive refinement), plus time measurements.

Q12_statistical_analysis.justification: User study includes median Dice with standard deviations and Wilcoxon tests with p-values.

Q13_comparison_sota.justification: Compares against SAM, SAM2, SAM-Med2D, MedSAM, ScribblePrompt, SAM-Med3D, and SegVol.

Q14_per_organ_results.justification: Per-structure results reported for expert scribble benchmark (LV, RV, MYO), but not for all datasets in main benchmark.

Q15_limitations.justification: Discusses limitations of existing methods and notes points as weakest prompt type, but no dedicated failure case analysis.

risk_of_bias.selection_bias: Medium - Patient selection not explicitly defined; relies on publicly available datasets which may not represent all clinical scenarios.
risk_of_bias.performance_bias: Low - Consistent evaluation protocol (RadioActive benchmark) and metrics used across all models.
risk_of_bias.reporting_bias: Low - Key outcomes (Dice, AUC, time, user study) reported; some per-organ results omitted but not selectively.

detailed_extraction.title: nnInteractive: Redefining 3D Promptable Segmentation
detailed_extraction.authors: Fabian Isensee, Maximilian Rokuss, Lars Krämer, Stefan Dinkelacker, Ashis Ravindran, Florian Stritzke, Benjamin Hamm, Tassilo Wald, Moritz Langenberg, Constantin Ulrich, Jonathan Deissler, Ralf Floca, Klaus Maier-Hein

contribution_summary.main_contribution: Introduces nnInteractive, the first comprehensive 3D interactive open-set segmentation model supporting diverse prompts (points, scribbles, boxes, lasso) and trained on 120+ multimodal datasets, integrated into Napari and MITK.
contribution_summary.novelty: Combines early prompting in a 3D U-Net, a novel lasso prompt, AutoZoom for large structures, and large-scale training with SuperVoxels to achieve state-of-the-art performance and usability.
strengths: Unprecedented training scale (64,518 volumes, 120+ datasets)
Supports multiple prompt types including lasso, enabling intuitive 2D interactions for 3D segmentation
Strong performance across diverse modalities and out-of-distribution datasets
User study demonstrates expert-level accuracy and 72% time reduction
Publicly available with integration into established platforms
weaknesses: Loss function not specified or justified
Training hyperparameters not fully disclosed
Per-organ results not reported for all benchmark datasets
Selection bias possible due to reliance on public datasets
contribution_summary.clinical_applicability: High - Integrated into Napari and MITK, supports real-time interactive segmentation with <10GB VRAM, and user study shows expert-level accuracy with significant time savings, making it suitable for clinical workflows.
